units.title: The Cold Kitchen
units.blurb: Salads and dressings, cold appetizers and canapés.

units.title: Preserving and Charcuterie
units.blurb: Quick pickles, confit and terrines, cured meats and cheese, as they are described and served.

topics.title: Salads and Dressings
topics.short: Wash and dry greens well, dress them just before serving; a vinaigrette is about 3 parts oil to 1 part acid, and emulsified dressings stay mixed.
topics.trouble: Cooks dress wet greens, so the dressing slides off and pools at the bottom.

topics.title: Canapés and Hors d'Oeuvres
topics.short: A canapé is a base, a spread and a topping, small enough for one or two bites; cold food stays at 41°F or below until it is served.
topics.trouble: Cooks build canapés hours early on bread, which goes soggy.

topics.title: Quick Pickles and Refrigerator Pickles
topics.short: Vegetables in a vinegar brine, kept in the refrigerator. Canning for the shelf is a separate skill: use only tested recipes from USDA or extension services.
topics.trouble: People invent a low-vinegar recipe and keep it on the shelf; only tested recipes are safe for canning.

topics.title: Confit, Pâtés and Terrines
topics.short: Confit is meat cooked slowly in fat; a terrine is a seasoned meat or vegetable mixture cooked in a mold and served cold. Both are kept refrigerated.
topics.trouble: People think fat-covered confit keeps at room temperature; keep it in the refrigerator.

topics.title: Charcuterie and Cheese Boards
topics.short: What dry-cured ham and salami are, why their making needs exact curing salts and controlled rooms, and how to build and serve a board of cured meats and cheese.
topics.trouble: Home cooks try to dry-cure sausage by guesswork; curing needs measured curing salt and controlled temperature and humidity.
